name: Sega SG-1000
description: Sega's first home video game console, a Z80-based cartridge system released in Japan in July 1983. It led directly to the Mark III and the Master System, starting Sega's line of home hardware.
curiosities: It went on sale in Japan on 15 July 1983, the same day as Nintendo's Famicom.
Sega sold a home-computer sibling, the SC-3000, that ran the same cartridges.
Its video chip is the same TMS9918 family used in the ColecoVision and MSX computers.
Its successor, the SG-1000 Mark III, was redesigned as the Master System for the West.
SG stands for Sega Game; the console was Sega's first for the home.
Sega expected to sell about 50,000 in its first year and sold some 160,000.
The original's joystick is wired to the console; the SG-1000 II of 1984 has two detachable pads.
It has only 1 KB of RAM for games, with 16 KB more for the picture.
Credit-card-sized Sega Card games played through the Card Catcher, an adapter in the cartridge slot.
Girl's Garden, an SG-1000 game of 1984, was the first game Yuji Naka programmed, years before Sonic.
Tsukuda Original sold a licensed version, the Othello Multivision, that plays its games.
The Mark III that followed it plays its cartridges and cards too.
story: Sega's first home console, the SG-1000, launched in Japan on 15 July 1983, the same day as Nintendo's Famicom.
It sold respectably, mostly ports of Sega's arcade games, but the Famicom pulled far ahead.
Its successors, the Mark III and the Master System, kept the same base and improved on it.
